This is bunker. You label an issue, and you get back a pull request that has been reviewed, tested, and merged. It runs A I coding agents in locked down sandboxes, and only lets their work in when it passes review and your tests.

The idea is simple. Your backlog gets worked on while you do something else. A I agents can write good code, but running them on your own machine, with your passwords, and merging whatever they write, is a risk. Bunker is the harness around the agent. A sandbox to work in, a second A I to review, your tests as the gate, and GitHub's own rules deciding what merges.

Here is one issue, start to finish. You pick a job by labelling a GitHub issue. Bunker checks the label really came from a maintainer. An A I writes the change in a sandbox, on its own branch. A second A I reviews it, and sends it back if something is wrong. Bunker runs your tests, and if they fail, the agent gets one round to fix them. Then GitHub's required checks pass, and auto merge lands it. If the change touches bunker's own rules, it waits for you. If it can't finish, it says why.

You can leave it running. It works through the queue in priority order, bugs first, two issues at a time, each in its own sandbox. It keeps open pull requests green, fixing failed checks and resolving conflicts. It has daily and monthly spend caps, a live view, desktop notifications, and a status command, so you can check in whenever you like.

It is built to be left alone. Only a maintainer's label queues work, and issues edited after they were labelled are refused. Comments from strangers never reach the agent. The agent never sees your GitHub token or your S S H keys, and the repository's git internals are read only inside the sandbox. Tests run with no network and no credentials. Changes to C I, to bunker's config, or to the agent's instructions wait for a person. Nothing merges without a required check on GitHub. And every one of these safety gates has a test that fails if it ever breaks.

Bunker built itself. In two days, it wrote and merged one hundred and forty seven pull requests to its own repository, against twenty three written by hand. It now has almost seven hundred tests guarding about eight thousand eight hundred lines of code, at an average agent cost of about one dollar fifteen per merged issue. Main stayed green apart from one flaky test window, since fixed, with no reverts.

Bunker was inspired by sandcastle. Sandcastle is a toolkit for building agent loops, with many agents and sandbox providers to choose from. Bunker is one finished, opinionated loop, from issue to merged pull request, with the queue, review, merge and unattended safety already built in.

Next is version one. The contract is done: subcommands, one config style, and a trimmed library. So is the reliability work: a fix round after failed tests, a test hygiene guard, and a pull request shepherd. Now comes a two week soak, running unattended on bunker and on another real repository. When the reliability bar holds for the whole window, it gets tagged one point oh.
You choose the work. Bunker does it safely. Label an issue, and come back to a reviewed, tested, merged pull request, or a clear reason why not.
